title: Investigating OpenAI’s ChatGPT Potentials in Generating Chatbot's Dialogue for English as a Foreign Language Learning
venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether OpenAI’s ChatGPT can generate suitable dialogue materials for use in an English as a Foreign Language (EFL) chatbot system. The motivating problem is that EFL students often have limited opportunities to practice spoken English, and chatbot-based practice depends heavily on the quality and appropriateness of the reference dialogues used. The authors argue that human-created dialogue materials are time-consuming to produce, so they investigate whether generative AI can create usable alternatives.

The study does not test learning outcomes in a classroom trial. Instead, it generates dialogue materials with ChatGPT for a mobile voice-enabled EFL practice application and evaluates those materials using readability metrics. The prompt frames the dialogue as a conversation between an undergraduate student and an exchange student from Italy across 15 everyday topics, with multiple alternative responses per line. The authors then create 450 unique dialogue samples and analyze them using Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall, and McAlpine EFLAW readability formulas to estimate their difficulty and suitability for learners.

The population represented in the generated dialogues is undergraduate students, and the institutional context is Tokyo Denki University in Japan, although this is primarily a content-generation and text-analysis study rather than a participant-based intervention study. The mobile app context is described as supporting listening, reading, and speaking practice through text-to-speech, speech recognition, and read-aloud interaction, but no experimental deployment with student outcome data is reported in this paper.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated dialogues appear linguistically appropriate for lower-level EFL learners, especially those around CEFR A2, with some materials also offering useful vocabulary challenge for B1-level content. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise for generating understandable, varied reference dialogue for EFL chatbot systems. However, the paper provides no direct causal evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes, no randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation, and no measured effects on phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary acquisition, or reading comprehension.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical but non-causal evaluation using readability analyses of generated materials, with no randomized or quasi-experimental design and no direct learner outcome testing. It provides limited evidence about suitability of content rather than educational effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful dialogue materials for EFL learners, but impact on student outcomes is unclear because no learning gains, behavioral changes, or classroom effects were estimated. For the targeted verification question, this is a near-miss rather than direct causal evidence on K-12 foundational reading.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT to generate reference dialogues and alternative reply lines for an EFL chatbot intended to support learners' dialogue practice and speaking activities.
A mobile voice-enabled chatbot application delivers the generated dialogues for listening, read-aloud, and speaking practice with text-to-speech and speech recognition support.
ChatGPT is used as a language-content generation tool to produce readable English dialogue materials tailored for EFL learners.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that ChatGPT-generated dialogues appear suitable for EFL dialogue practice materials, especially for CEFR A2 learners, based on readability analyses of 450 simulated dialogue combinations. Findings are based on text readability metrics rather than learner performance outcomes; no causal evidence on speaking, listening, or fluency gains was collected, and no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Readability of generated dialogue materials using Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall, and McAlpine EFLAW metrics
finding.study_size: 450 simulated dialogue samples derived from 15 topics

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generated dialogues were generally easy to comprehend and suitable for learners around CEFR A2, with some B1-level materials offering vocabulary stimulation. However, this is an indirect text-complexity finding based on readability formulas, not direct evidence on K-12 foundational reading outcomes such as phonemic awareness, phonics, decoding, oral reading fluency, vocabulary growth, or reading comprehension.
finding.measure: Text readability and inferred comprehensibility/vocabulary suitability of ChatGPT-generated EFL dialogues
finding.study_size: 450 simulated dialogue samples derived from 15 topics
